GILD Austin Event: a room of engineering leaders working through something most teams feel but haven't named the comprehension gap.

AI has decoupled how fast we ship from how well we understand what we shipped. Pre-AI, understanding was baked into the build process slow, but built in. Now delivery has outpaced comprehension, and the cost that used to hide inside the build cycle is sitting out in the open.

Our conversation starter, Ivan Pointer (Senior Director of Engineering, NetRise), walked the room through a live case study a two-phase RBAC rewrite where phase one shipped clean, and phase two stalled entirely: thousands of lines of spec churn, dozens of commits, most of them reverts. Not because the team got worse. Because the agents and the humans were now contending with a system too large to hold in their heads.

The best ideas in the room were ownership structures: engineers accountable for what they ship, constraint limits on how much a single PR can touch, weekly sessions where the team has to explain their own code out loud.

The room brought together leaders from companies including Oracle, Dell Technologies, Global Payments, Sonar, SmartAsset, Atlassian, and others across AI, software, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology.

The open question on the table: how do you keep development deterministic when "done" becomes a vibe instead of a test case.

When there's a gold rush, the people selling shovels win.

That is how Anand frames the bottom of the AI stack on the GILD Podcast. Everyone is fighting at the model and app layers, but the durable value sits underneath: the compute, the chips, the data centers, the raw energy and resources most software people never think about.

He goes as far as calling resources "L minus one," the layer so foundational nobody in software even touches it. It is the same story that made NVIDIA the winner of this cycle.

If you are building in AI, it is worth asking which layer you actually live on, and how far you are from the shovels.

The full conversation with Anand Arivukkarasu is live now. Listen here: https://lnkd.in/g6JvBUmK

contentItems.title:
Which verticals do the big AI labs take over first? Anand has a clear answer: MarTech is first on the clock.

On the GILD Podcast, he lays out the logic. MarTech is lightly regulated, runs on data that is already everywhere, and the models have trained on trillions of those data points. Low friction, easy to absorb.

MedTech is the opposite. Heavy compliance, gated data the labs cannot simply reach. That regulatory wall is exactly what buys those categories time.

The pattern is worth sitting with: regulation and data access are quietly deciding who gets disrupted next, and who is protected.

New episode drops tomorrow. Which vertical do you think falls after MarTech?
